lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- The Interview Warm-Up
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flavio Gattaz | Lesson 11 -- The Interview Warm-Up
lesson.grammar_point: indirect questions and clarification requests (could you tell me, I was wondering whether, would you mind repeating)

listenings.text: People think the first five minutes are a courtesy, and they are not. What I am measuring in that part is whether you can hold an ordinary conversation in English, at normal speed, about nothing in particular, because that is what a classroom is made of. Nobody learns anything in a seminar by making prepared speeches. Here is the thing that surprises candidates. In a whole admissions season, almost nobody asks me to repeat anything. Half of those people understood every word and half of them did not, and I cannot tell which half I am talking to, so I start to distrust all the answers, including the good ones. The sentence I am always glad to hear is would you mind rephrasing that. It costs the candidate nothing, it takes four seconds, and it tells me the person in front of me is actually listening to me rather than performing at me. I have never once written that down as a negative.

It happened twice in the same interview and I handled it two completely different ways. The first time, she asked a long question, and somewhere in the second half of it I stopped following. I still heard the words. I just could not hold the shape of the question any more. And I guessed. I gave a confident, well organised answer to something she had not asked, and I watched her write something down while I was talking. The second time it happened I did the thing I had been afraid of all week. I said I was sorry, I had not caught the last part, and could she say it again. She said it again, shorter. I answered it. The whole exchange took about six seconds. What I had got wrong was thinking that asking for repetition would sound weak. The weak thing was the confident answer to the wrong question. Nobody in that room was grading my ears.

On a normal video call the delay between one person speaking and the other person hearing it sits somewhere between a fifth of a second and half a second. That sounds like nothing, and it is enough to change a conversation. It is why two people start talking at the same time and then both stop, and it is why an ordinary pause for thought reads as hesitation to the person at the other end. Researchers who recorded several hundred of these calls found something more uncomfortable for anybody working in a second language. Those speakers waited longer before taking their turn, and they asked for repetition less often on video than they did on the telephone, and the report is blunt about it: both of those habits make a competent speaker sound less sure than they are. The advice at the end of the study is two lines long. Start your first three words slightly early, so the line belongs to you. And when you need something repeated, ask in a full sentence rather than a noise, because a full sentence survives the delay and a noise does not.
